issues.legal_issue: Ancestral property allotted to a sole surviving coparcener in partition is separate property while he remains the sole coparcener, but becomes coparcenary property when a son is subsequently born to him.
material_facts: The father received ancestral property in a partition while he was unmarried and the sole surviving coparcener in respect of that property.
The plaintiff was born to the father after the partition.
issues.conclusion: The property was the father's separate property until the plaintiff was born; upon the plaintiff's birth, it became coparcenary property in which the plaintiff acquired an interest.
issues.legal_principle: A sole surviving coparcener may treat property allotted to him in partition as his separate property, but the coparcenary revives when a son is born to him, and the son then acquires an interest in the property. The Court relied on M. Yogendra v. Leelamma, (2009) 15 SCC 184. It distinguished Bhanwar Singh v. Puran, (2008) 3 SCC 87, because that case concerned succession, whereas this case concerned the status of a son in relation to his father and property allotted on partition. The Court also noted the pre-amendment position under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, that male members acquired an interest in coparcenary property by birth.

rule.if: civil_appeal_in_property_dispute and ancestral_property_allotted_in_partition and recipient_was_sole_surviving_coparcener and son_born_after_partition

predicates.civil_appeal_in_property_dispute: The matter came before the court as a civil appeal concerning rights in property.
predicates.ancestral_property_allotted_in_partition: An ancestor's property was allotted to a person in a partition.
predicates.recipient_was_sole_surviving_coparcener: The person who received the property was the only surviving coparcener in relation to it.
predicates.son_born_after_partition: A son was born to the recipient after the partition.

issues.definition: When a civil property appeal concerns ancestral property allotted to a sole surviving coparcener and a son is born to him afterward, the rule means that the property becomes coparcenary property.

issues.legal_issue: A father's alienation of coparcenary property after a son is born is invalid to the extent of the coparcenary property when it is not made for legal necessity.
material_facts: After the plaintiff's birth, his father executed sale deeds and a release deed affecting the property.
The father had been the sole surviving coparcener until the plaintiff was born, after which the plaintiff acquired an interest in the property.
The parties did not claim that the father executed the deeds as karta for legal necessity.
issues.conclusion: The sale deeds and release deed were illegal, null and void to the extent of the entire coparcenary property; the parties could pursue remedies in an appropriate proceeding regarding the property that would have fallen to the father's share when the deeds were executed.
issues.legal_principle: After a son is born and acquires an interest in property that had been held by his father as a sole surviving coparcener, the father may alienate the coparcenary property only as karta for legal necessity. An alienation made before the son's birth cannot be challenged by the son on that basis, but a post-birth alienation without legal necessity is invalid as to the coparcenary property. The Court applied the principle supported by M. Yogendra v. Leelamma, (2009) 15 SCC 184.

rule.if: civil_appeal_in_property_dispute and son_acquired_interest_by_birth and father_alienated_property_after_son_birth and not alienation_for_legal_necessity

predicates.civil_appeal_in_property_dispute: The matter came before the court as a civil appeal concerning rights in property.
predicates.son_acquired_interest_by_birth: A son was born while his father held property allotted from ancestral property, and the son thereby acquired an interest in it.
predicates.father_alienated_property_after_son_birt: The father transferred or released property after the son was born.
predicates.alienation_for_legal_necessity: The father made the transfer as manager of the family property for a necessary family purpose.

issues.definition: When a civil property appeal involves a son who acquired an interest by birth and his father alienated the property afterward without doing so for legal necessity, the rule means that the alienation is invalid as to the coparcenary property.
